newsitem.title: UK: Major in last ditch effort to avoid poll disaster.
newsitem.headline: Major in last ditch effort to avoid poll disaster.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major began a whirlwind tour of Britain on Monday in what looked increasingly like a doomed attempt to save his Conservative government from defeat in Thursday's election.

With opinion polls, pro-Conservative newspapers and even one of the ruling party's MPs predicting an overwhelming victory for the new-look Labour Party, Major flew first to Northern Ireland, the province whose problems have bedevilled his premiership.
Labour leader Tony Blair tried to dampen down the euphoria of supporters who, inspired by weekend media stories, believe the election is in the bag.
"This election is not over until it is over. The only poll that counts is the election. I don't think this is a landslide country," Blair told a news conference in Nottingham, central England.
The latest poll on Monday gave Labour a 19-point lead over the Conservatives, barely changed from March 17 when Major announced a six-week election campaign -- the longest for 80 years.

If the opinion polls are right then Labour, out of office since 1979 when Margaret Thatcher swept to power, would win the biggest majority in its history -- around 150 seats in the 659-seat House of Commons.
Labour needs a uniform 4.3 percent swing among Britain's 44 million voters to achieve victory.

The optimism of pro-Conservative newspapers which last week rejoiced at the one poll of the campaign to put the Conservatives within striking distance of Labour -- just five points behind -- has melted away. In its place is an increasing interest in a post-election battle for the party's leadership.
"Tories battle to halt election wipeout", said the Daily Mail. The headline of its rival, the Express, read: "Major's last bid to avert disaster".

Conservative MP Edwina Currie, one of the dwindling band of pro-Europeans in an increasingly anti-Brussels party, provoked the fury of colleagues by predicting a Labour majority of at least 100 seats in a Sunday newspaper.

Sir Marcus Fox, chairman of the Conservatives' influential 1922 committee of rank-and-file MPs, dismissed Currie as "a loose cannon, firing in all directions", but her forecast only deepened the sense of foreboding at Conservative headquarters.
In an interview with the Daily Telegraph, Major insisted the polls, the atmosphere in the country was similar to that in 1992 when Britain's electors gave him a surprise 21-seat majority.
"There is no feeling of hostility, no great feeling for radical change," he said. "It doesn't have that feel about it at all -- and I have contested quite a few elections now."

Blair, who has led his party to the centre ground of politics in the three years of his leadership, jettisoning traditional tax-and-spend policies, is benefitting from deep divisions within the Conservatives, notably over Europe.

Blair accused the ruling party of "weakness, division and drift" and claimed that if it won a fifth consecutive term of office, Britain's National Health Service would be next in line for the privatising zeal that it has shown.

Major's Northern Ireland visit, amid heavy security, underlined his determination not to allow the Irish Republican Army to disrupt polling day, despite recent bomb warnings which have brought chaos to British motorways and railways.
In Scotland and Wales, aides said, Major plans to push the message that Labour's plans for constitutional change could imperil the unity of Britain.

In an otherwise cautious manifesto, Blair has set out radical plans for mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales, reform of the unelected upper House of Lords and other measures such as a Freedom of Information Bill.
